summary: Specifies the conventions for using the Advanced Encryption Standard to encrypt content in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS is a format for signed and encrypted email. RFC 3565 tells it how to use AES, the modern cipher that replaced DES. It fixes the identifiers that mean "AES with a 128-bit key" and the rules for safely handing the content key to each recipient.

questions: how does cms encrypt content with aes
which aes key sizes does cms support
subtitle: How to use AES to encrypt message content in the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and how the content key is wrapped for each recipient.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax needed agreed conventions for using the newer AES cipher as its content encryption algorithm, replacing the older DES.
tldr.mechanism: AES in CBC mode encrypts the content under a random content-encryption key, and that key is wrapped for each recipient by RSA key transport, Diffie-Hellman key agreement, a previously shared key or a password-derived key.
tldr.outcome: It defines the object identifiers for AES-CBC and the AES key wrap with 128, 192 and 256-bit keys, and the S/MIME capability encodings that let clients announce AES support.

facts.label: Key wrap output
facts.value: 64 bits longer than the content key

facts.label: Key wrap cost
facts.value: 6*n AES operations, n blocks of 64 bits

today: RFC 3565 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2003, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains the document that registers the AES object identifiers for use with the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
This document specifies the conventions for using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) as a content encryption algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) enveloped-data and encrypted-data content types. CMS values are generated using ASN.1, using the Basic Encoding Rules and the Distinguished Encoding Rules.

The CMS enveloped-data content type consists of encrypted content and wrapped content-encryption keys for one or more recipients. The encrypted-data content type consists of encrypted content with implicit key management, where the key is shared in some other way. AES is used to encrypt the content in both cases.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS messages can hold encrypted content. RFC 3565 pins down exactly how AES is used in that, so two implementations encrypt the same way.

sections.title: The AES Algorithm
sections.content:
AES was developed to replace DES. The AES Federal Information Processing Standard specifies a cryptographic algorithm for use by U.S. Government organizations, but it is also expected to be widely used by organizations, institutions and individuals outside the U.S. Government.

Two researchers who developed and submitted the Rijndael algorithm for consideration are both cryptographers from Belgium: Dr. Joan Daemen of Proton World International and Dr. Vincent Rijmen. NIST selected Rijndael for AES because it offers a combination of security, performance, efficiency, ease of implementation and flexibility. Its key setup time is excellent and its key agility is good, its very low memory requirements make it well suited to restricted-space environments, and its operations are among the easiest to defend against power and timing attacks.

The AES specifies three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: AES is the cipher that replaced DES. It comes in three key sizes and is fast and small enough to run on small devices.

sections.title: Enveloped-data Conventions
sections.content:
Compliant software MUST meet the requirements for constructing an enveloped-data content type stated in the CMS document. The AES content-encryption key MUST be randomly generated for each instance of an enveloped-data content type, and that key is what encrypts the content.

The EnvelopedData version is determined by the algorithm given in the CMS document. The recipientInfos choice depends on the key management technique used, and the contentEncryptionAlgorithm field MUST specify a symmetric encryption algorithm. Implementations MUST support content encryption with AES, but MAY support other algorithms as well. The unprotectedAttrs field MAY be present.
sections.plainLanguage: For every message, a fresh random content key is generated and used to encrypt the text. The message then records which algorithm was used and how the key should be delivered to each reader.

sections.title: Four Ways to Deliver the Content Key
sections.content:
AES can be used with the enveloped-data content type with any of four key management techniques. With key transport, the AES content-encryption key is uniquely wrapped for each recipient using the recipient's public RSA key and other values. The recipient's certificate MUST contain an RSA public key, the keyEncryptionAlgorithm field specifies the key transport algorithm, and the encryptedKey field is the result of encrypting the content key with the recipient's RSA public key. The KeyTransRecipientInfo version MUST be either 0 or 2, depending on whether the certificate is named by issuer and serial number or by subject key identifier.

With key agreement, the content key is uniquely wrapped for each recipient using a pairwise symmetric key-encryption key generated from an originator's randomly generated private key (ES-DH) or previously generated private key (SS-DH), the recipient's public Diffie-Hellman key, and other values. The KeyAgreeRecipient version MUST be 3, the originatorInfo field MUST be the originatorKey alternative holding the originator's ephemeral public key, the keyEncryptionAlgorithm MUST be the id-alg-ESDH identifier, and the ukm field MAY be present.

With a previously distributed symmetric key, the content key is wrapped using a symmetric KEK that was distributed earlier, such as a mail list key, and the KEKRecipientInfo choice MUST be used. With password encryption, the content key is wrapped using a KEK derived from a password or other shared secret, and the PasswordRecipientInfo choice MUST be used. In both cases the keyEncryptionAlgorithm field MUST be one of the AES wrap identifiers and its parameters field MUST be absent.
sections.plainLanguage: The content key has to reach each reader somehow. The RFC allows four routes: encrypt it to the reader's RSA public key, agree on it with Diffie-Hellman, use a key already shared out of band, or derive it from a password.

sections.title: The AES Key Wrap Algorithm
sections.content:
The AES key wrap algorithm encrypts one AES key inside another AES key. Its output is 64 bits longer than the input content key, and the additional bits are a checksum. The algorithm uses 6*n AES encryption and decryption operations, where n is the number of 64-bit blocks in the content key.

NIST has assigned three object identifiers for the AES key wrap algorithm: id-aes128-wrap, id-aes192-wrap and id-aes256-wrap. In all cases the parameters field MUST be absent. The object identifier gives the size of the key-encryption key but says nothing about the size of the wrapped content key. Implementations MUST support the case where the content key and the key-encryption key have the same length. If different lengths are supported, the key-encryption key MUST be of equal or greater length than the content key.
sections.plainLanguage: The key wrap algorithm is what encrypts the content key with another key. It adds a checksum and takes a fixed number of AES operations per block, so its cost is predictable.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
AES is added to the set of symmetric content encryption algorithms defined in the CMS algorithms document. The AES content-encryption algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining mode is identified for the three key sizes by the object identifiers id-aes128-CBC, id-aes192-CBC and id-aes256-CBC.

The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain an AES-IV, defined as an octet string of size 16. The content encryption algorithm identifiers are located in the contentEncryptionAlgorithm fields of the enveloped-data and encrypted-data structures, and the algorithms are used to encrypt the content in the matching encryptedContent fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Each AES variant gets its own identifier, and the identifier always carries a 16-octet initialisation vector. A reader uses the identifier to work out the key size and the mode of operation.

sections.title: S/MIME Capability Attributes
sections.content:
An S/MIME client SHOULD announce the set of cryptographic functions it supports by using the S/MIME capabilities attribute. That attribute provides a partial list of object identifiers of cryptographic functions and MUST be signed by the client. The algorithm identifiers SHOULD be logically separated into functional categories and MUST be ordered with respect to the client's preference.

If an S/MIME client is required to support symmetric encryption with AES, the capabilities attribute MUST contain the AES object identifier in the category of symmetric algorithms, and the parameter with this encoding MUST be absent. The encodings for the mandatory key sizes are listed in the RFC: the 128-bit capability, a 196-bit capability, and the 256-bit capability.

When a sending agent creates an encrypted message it has to decide which encryption algorithm to use. In general that decision involves information from the capabilities lists included in messages received from the recipient, as well as private agreements, user preferences and legal restrictions. If users require AES for symmetric encryption, the S/MIME clients on both the sending and receiving side MUST support it and it MUST be set in the user preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail client should say which ciphers it supports, in a signed list attached to its messages. The sender then picks the strongest cipher both sides have in common.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If RSA-OAEP and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 are both used to transport the same content key, an attacker can still mount the Bleichenbacher attack against the RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 encrypted key. It is generally unadvisable to mix both in the same set of recipients.

Implementations must protect the RSA private key and the content key. Compromise of the RSA private key may result in the disclosure of all messages protected with that key, and compromise of the content key may result in disclosure of the associated encrypted content.

The generation of AES content keys relies on random numbers. Using inadequate pseudo-random number generators can result in little or no security, because an attacker may find it much easier to reproduce the generator environment that produced the keys and search the resulting small set of possibilities than brute force search the whole key space. RFC 1750 offers important guidance in this area.

When wrapping a content key with a key-encryption key, the key-encryption key MUST always be at least the same length as the content key. An attacker will generally work at the weakest point in an encryption system, and that would be the smaller of the two key sizes for a brute force attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mistakes would weaken the scheme: mixing two RSA padding schemes for the same key, and using a weak random number generator for the content key. The wrapping key must never be shorter than the key it wraps.

viz.caption: THE FOUR KEY MANAGEMENT TECHNIQUES ALLOWED FOR AES IN CMS

columns: How the content-encryption key is protected

cells: Uniquely wrapped for each recipient with the recipient's RSA public key
Wrapped with a pairwise KEK from Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral-static or static-static
Wrapped with a KEK that was shared earlier, such as a mail list key
Wrapped with a KEK derived from a password or other shared secret
